doc.title: Warren Vaché interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 23, 1995

chapter: Sound, electronics and the changing scene
title: Why the cornet; individual sound; Sweets Edison
summary: He plays cornet because it is his voice; sound as personality, and admiration for Sweets Edison's uniqueness.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: What led you — I’m going to turn back the clock a little bit — what led you to stick with the cornet? Is there any special reason for that?

Yeah, well, the other part of what I got from being around guys like Roy and Vic was that controlling your instrument and learning to play it well are only the beginning phase of being a musician. The sound that instrument makes has to become your voice, as natural as when you speak or sing. And just as idiomatic as the singing or speaking voice is, © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

that’s what your sound on the instrument is allowed to become in jazz. So the reason I play the cornet is because that’s what I hear, that is my voice. I’ve had 150 trumpets in my hand. They never feel as comfortable as a cornet does. Now I’m admittedly not looking to get work in studios where I’m going to make the sound the producer wants to hear. When you make this choice, you actually limit the sort of work you can take. I’m not going to go out and audition for the Hamilton College Symphony, because the sound I make is going to be unacceptable in that situation. But you make that decision. And part of the magic of jazz for me is that so much of a player’s personality is expressed in that sound. You hear Vic Dickinson, there’s never going to be another person in the world that’s going to make that sound. Truly and completely unique. I can hear two bars of Roy Eldridge and tell you who it is. I mean this is the sort of thing that really fascinated me and I think that my life is just a constant search to find where I am — in relation to what I’ve learned, what I know, where I’ve worked — to find that voice, that character that makes me unique.
Well you really echo the sentiments of some of the other fellows we’ve talked to, Al Grey and Sweets Edison, they said the same thing in different ways.
Did you get enough that you didn’t have to edit? He’s the funniest man in the world. I have to send him $65 a month, you know, because I steal so much of his stuff.

He said the same thing: he said that he doesn’t hear, well he wasn’t complaining. He said that today he doesn’t hear that striving for sound as much as when he was coming on, and that that was a big part of everyone’s goal.

Yeah. Strength for individuality. Now everybody has a lovely, schooled, technical, marvelous approach, and I can’t distinguish one of them from another. You got three notes of Sweets, I mean Sweets Edison invented himself. He’s one of the prime characters in America and always has been. I mean it’s funny, where the hell was I, I did some jazz party and they put a bunch of trumpet players on the stand and Sweets was with us. And we’re all up there sweating and popping veins and doing our level best to impress everybody, and Sweets comes up and goes “boop” and the audience melts. It’s like shooting fish in a barrel for him. You know he doesn’t even have to touch it, he’s just so unique that I mean that’s the sort of thing that really, one of these days, I’ll get there. That’s what I’m working for, you know?
